name: obligation-matrix
description: Regulation × obligation grid — state-marker cells encode applies / partial / exempt at a glance.
purpose: Use when many regimes need comparing across the same obligations. Cells carry the universal state-token grammar ([x] applies, [-] partial, [ ] exempt, [/] out of scope) shared with checklist / verdict-grid / roadmap.

heading.description: Slide heading framing what the matrix compares.

matrix.description: Markdown table — rows are regulations, columns are obligations. Use state markers ([x] / [-] / [ ] / [/]) in cells.

key.description: OPTIONAL label set renaming the marker key: `[{[x], In force}, {[ ], Not subject}]`, one inline-code span alone in its paragraph. The key is the MARKER you already type in a cell (`[x]` `[-]` `[ ]` `[/]`), brackets included — a bare space key collapses to empty and would drop its row. Naming a subset is the normal case; the rest keep the default words declared in this manifest's `labelSet`. The paragraph is consumed so it names the key rather than also printing above the grid.

legend.description: Optional trailing paragraph — what to take from the matrix, or a caveat about the placements. It no longer has to explain the markers: the key under the grid names them, derived from the ones the cells actually carry.

whenToUse.title: Many regimes, shared obligations
whenToUse.body: Three or more regulations or jurisdictions compared across the same set of duties. The grid lets the reader scan a row to know a regime and a column to know an obligation.

whenToUse.title: State markers, not values
whenToUse.body: Cells are pass/partial/fail/skip — the universal `[x]` / `[-]` / `[ ]` / `[/]` grammar. For textual cell values use `table`.

whenToUse.title: The key's words are a DEFAULT, not a fixed vocabulary
whenToUse.body: 'Applies' and 'Exempt' suit a compliance matrix; a licensing or diligence grid wants other words. Write a label set above the grid — `[{[x], In force}, {[ ], Not subject}]` — and those markers are renamed; the ones you do not name keep theirs. The defaults are declared in this manifest's `labelSet`, which is also what `lint:deck` checks your keys against.

whenToUse.title: Risk axis with heat
whenToUse.body: The `heat` variant flips the palette so applies (`[x]`) reads as alarm. Exempt (`[ ]`) cells resolve to the neutral state and are NOT recolored — they don't turn 'relief' green. Use when the matrix is read for exposure, not for coverage.

antiPatterns.title: Two regimes only
antiPatterns.body: Past one row vs another the grid loses its purpose. Use `compare-prose` or `table` for two-regime comparisons.

antiPatterns.title: Mixed cell content
antiPatterns.body: Don't mix state markers with prose values in the same matrix — the cell width has to grow to fit prose and the marker grid collapses. Pick one cell type.

antiPatterns.title: Restating the key in prose
antiPatterns.body: The grid now draws its own key — one named marker per state the cells actually carry — so a trailing sentence repeating 'filled = applies, half = partial' costs a line and can go stale against the markers on the slide. Rename the words with a label set instead; keep the paragraph for what the key cannot say.

commonMistakes.mistake: Keying a label set on the marker's NAME rather than the marker.
commonMistakes.fix: `[{applies, In force}]` binds to nothing and the row is dropped. A key is the marker exactly as a cell spells it — `[x]`, `[-]`, `[ ]`, `[/]` — brackets included. The brackets are load-bearing: a bare space key collapses to empty under the parser's whitespace tidy and would take the `[ ]` row with it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Explicitly left-aligning table columns (`:---`) instead of leaving alignment unspecified or writing `:---:`.
commonMistakes.fix: The matrix unconditionally centers every cell, so a plain column with no alignment markers still centers state-marker glyphs fine. Only an EXPLICIT `:---` left-align syntax breaks it — that emits an inline left-align style, which (being inline) overrides the component's own centering rule regardless of specificity.

variantDecisionRule.useWhen: Neutral, data-first cell chrome with no additional emphasis — reference tone.

The matrix should read as exposure — applies (`[x]`) reads as alarm — not just coverage for reference. Exempt (`[ ]`) cells resolve to a neutral state that `heat` does NOT re-color; they keep their default neutral ring rather than turning 'relief' green.
The regimes genuinely differ in kind and each deserves body-level breathing room as its own card rather than a strict grid cell.

The state should read as a word — a status label — rather than an iconographic mark. This requires authoring literal text (inline code or bold) per cell instead of the `[x]`/`[-]`/`[ ]` state-marker grammar — `pills`' word-styling only targets literal text, so a table still written with bracket markers keeps its icon-only marks (no word appears), though the cell padding and row-zebra shift anyway since `pills` restyles every cell regardless of content.
Each regime should read as its own horizontal band, emphasizing that it's a distinct regime rather than a rank in a list.

split.note: table's reader, for table's reason: a wide read-across grid cannot paginate out of HORIZONTAL overflow, so it RESHAPES -- each regime row becomes a card whose column headers become in-card labels. Landscape renders the native grid untouched. A ROW SLICE WAS TRIED FIRST AND MEASURED: `cover-paginate` with a `row` axis repeats the <thead> per page and keeps every state mark, which looked like the better answer -- and it took the gallery from 9 bad pages to 43, because slicing rows does not narrow six columns. That is the emulator's own rule (a vertical paginator never fixes a wide table) seen from the wrong end. Enrolled 2026-09-13 (owner's call) after measuring 9 of 10 gallery pages bad at portrait. NO `capacity` BLOCK: `cover-cards` reads `split.perPage`, and declaring an authoring band here is a separate decision about what authors are TOLD. The first cut invented 4/5/6 and the gallery contract caught it immediately -- the component's own sample and stress doc both hold SIX regimes, which its stress summary calls "the grid ceiling", so any band that admits the sample also admits the ceiling and says nothing. Same conclusion as `code`.

handles.note: The projection reads a row as `<label>: <cell>; <cell>.`, which no single element on the slide holds — so the cue hid. The row's first cell is the label it opens with.
